issue: Whether the federal jurisdictional status of a place (such as a federal prison's status under the special maritime and territorial jurisdiction) is a legal question the court decides, or an adjudicative fact the jury must find?

sides.position: Territorial jurisdictional status is a legal question the court may decide, separate from the jury's factual finding on where the crime occurred.
cases: United States v. Davis, 726 F.3d 362 (2d Cir. 2013)
United States v. Silvers, 129 F.4th 332 (6th Cir. 2025)
United States v. Love, 20 F.4th 407 (8th Cir. 2021)
United States v. Warren, 984 F.2d 325 (9th Cir. 1993)
United States v. Perez, No. 24-4039 (4th Cir. Aug. 12, 2025)

sides.position: Territorial jurisdictional status is an adjudicative fact for the jury, classified by its use in the case rather than by its nature.
cases: United States v. Bello, 194 F.3d 18 (1st Cir. 1999)

this_court: Court decides jurisdictional status as a legal question for the court, rejecting the First Circuit's Bello approach.
quote: Perez and our dissenting colleague instead rely on the First Circuit's minority approach of classifying facts about territorial jurisdiction as adjudicative.
cite: United States v. Jesse Perez, No. 24-4039 (4th Cir. 2025)
